content.title: What Happens in ‘The Drama’? That Shocking and Controversial Twist, Explained
content.text: Warning: Major spoilers from “The Drama” ahead…“Save the date.”That’s the tagline for “The Drama,” the new film starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson. When the movie revealed its first trailer months ago, the teaser showed Zendaya and Pattinson portraying an engaged couple who plan to tie the knot in a few days. The release of the trailer coincided with a fake engagement ad running in the Boston Globe in December.The promotional material featured a picture of the fictitious couple with the headline, “Emma Harwood and Charlie Thompson Engaged,” celebrating the happy pair. But “The Drama,” a comedy from director Kristoffer Borgli, didn’t appear to be a lighthearted, romantic flick about a couple preparing for their nuptials. Instead, the movie gave off a much darker tone as the first and second trailers teases a confession from Zendaya’s character so startling it causes Pattinson’s character to second guess their relationship. Robert Pattinson and Zendaya in "The Drama."Theories about the twist made fans want to “save the date” to see what kind of revelation could dismantle the foundation of a seemingly picture-perfect relationship. When “The Drama” arrived in theaters April 3, moviegoers finally learned the film’s big secret. In fact, the mystery is revealed early on in the film’s first act, causing every character to spiral and grapple with Emma’s past until the credits roll. Want to know what Emma was hiding from her fiancé? Read on to find out how “The Drama,” which will surely be one of the most controversial films of the year, ends. What Is the Big Twist in ‘The Drama’? Leading up to Emma and Charlie’s big day, the characters go to a wedding menu tasting with their best man and matron of honor, married couple Mike (Mamoudou Athie) and Rachel (Alana Haim). As the couples become inebriated, Rachel challenges them all to reveal the worst act they’ve ever committed. Mike goes first, sharing that he used his ex-girlfriend as a human shield when they encountered a dangerous dog. Rachel admits that when she was a child she locked a boy in a closet in an abandoned RV and left him there for hours. Next, Charlie confesses to cyberbullying another child when he was a teenager. Finally, it is Emma’s turn to own up to her greatest sin. She tells her fiancé and friends that she planned a school shooting when she was a teenager, but she later decided not to go through with it. Initially, Charlie, Mike and Rachel assume Emma is joking. But once she includes more details, like stealing her father’s rifle to commit the crime, they realize she is being honest about her violent past. Mike is stunned and Rachel becomes enraged, pointing out that her cousin uses a wheelchair because she was the victim of gun violence. As for Charlie, he starts to fear Emma and questions her every move, wondering if the teenager version of her still exists. How Does ‘The Drama’ End?Charlie continues to unravel as the movie progresses. He questions if he should marry Emma and if she is the same person he fell in love with. Before the wedding, he kisses his co-worker Misha (Hailey Gates) but stops himself before they go any further. The wedding day arrives. At the reception, Emma is anxious Rachel will confront her about the secret in her matron of honor speech. She also tells Charles that she has noticed Misha behaving strangely, so she asks her to come speak with them privately. Misha, assuming Emma knows about Charlie cheating, immediately blurts out that they kissed. Then, Charlie gives an awkward speech where he shares inappropriate details about his relationship with Emma in front of their friends and family. While he is speaking, Misha’s boyfriend Blake (Michael Abbott Jr.), who has just been informed about the infidelity, approaches Charlie and headbutts him. The scene cuts to a bloodied and bruised Charlie returning to his apartment alone the night of the wedding. He tries to find Emma and goes to one of their favorite diners to see if she is there. He arrives, still wearing his bloodstained tuxedo, orders and sits down. Moments later, Emma walks in wearing her wedding dress. She initially ignores him and buys food before taking a seat across from Charlie in a booth. The two attempt to start over and get to know each other again before the movie ends. Reactions to ‘The Drama’In addition to “The Drama” tackling the subject of mass shootings and the psyche behind those who plan the violent crimes, the movie includes scenes of Emma, both as an adult and a child, posing with rifles. It also shows teenage Emma recording a manifesto video in which she lists the classmates she plans to target. Another uncomfortable scene pops up when an adult Charlie embraces the teenage version of Emma. Given the sensitive subject matter and controversial scenes, the film has already received backlash. Ahead of the release, March for Our Lives, an organization that works to end gun violence, posted a statement on Instagram that called out the film for being marketed in a way that “is deeply misaligned with the reality it engages.”The organization wrote, in part, “We understand that art can provoke discomfort and use humor to approach difficult subjects. But when something like a school shooting is treated lightly or played for irony, it raises a deeper question: what kind of conversation is this meant to start?”At the end of the statement, the organization said, “We expect better from A24 and the artists behind it. What Have Critics Said About ‘The Drama’? The reviews of the film have been favorable, with the movie certified fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Los Angeles Times reviewer Amy Nicholson said, “(Borgli) uses shock tactics the way little children throw lollipops onto anthills — he just wants to cause a stir. If his apathy offends anyone in the audience, I suspect he doesn’t care about that, either. I feel equally detached about his coldly amusing film but I admire his intentions. His focus is on the fallout.” Natalia Keogan of AV Club wrote, “The film is less about confronting a pervasive social issue than it is interrogating how much we actually know about our partners — or any loved one, really — and if full transparency is actually a productive mode of intimacy.”But Nick Schager of the Daily Beast wasn’t a fan of how the story was told and the movie’s style. “Not that anyone survives ‘The Drama,’ which is so misguided, empty, and unfunny that, like Emma’s scary indiscretion, it should have never seen the light of day,” he said. Roger Ebert reviewer Robert Daniels describes the movie as “juvenile.” He said the film “hopes to humanize (Charlie and Emma) as complex people meant for one another and to demonize those critical of them as self-righteous hypocrites. But what gives this glib, circuitous film the right to persecute the apathetic when it barely understands its own characters?”
